docs.title: pinhook
docs.text:
The pluggable python framework for IRC bots and Twitch bots.

You write small plugins, each one a python function, and pinhook handles connecting, joining channels, ops, bans and getting your replies back to the right place.

import pinhook.plugin

@pinhook.plugin.command('!hello')
def hello(msg):
    return pinhook.plugin.message('hi {}!'.format(msg.nick))

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install pinhook

Make a plugins folder, save the plugin above in it as hello.py, then start a bot:

from pinhook.bot import Bot

bot = Bot(
    channels=['#foo'],
    nickname='ph-bot',
    server='irc.libera.chat',
    port=6697,
    ssl_required=True,
)
bot.start()

Say !hello in #foo and the bot answers.

docs.title: Where to next
docs.text:
• Getting started: config files, the command line tool and your first plugin
  • Options: everything you can set on a bot
  • Writing plugins: commands, listeners and what a plugin gets to work with
  • Testing plugins: check your plugins with pytest, no server needed
  • Bans and ops: who can run what, and bans that are hard to dodge
  • Troubleshooting: what the log messages mean
  • Coming from an older version? See Upgrading to 1.11, and Preparing for 2.0 to get your plugins ready for what's next

pinhook is made with love on tilde.town. Live bots using it include pinhook-tilde and adminbot.

docs.title: Bans and ops
docs.text: ops decides who can run op-only commands, and banned_users who the bot ignores. Both take the same three kinds of entry.

docs.title: Kinds of entry
docs.text:
Entry Example Matches How hard to dodge Nick troll that nick, in any case easy: anyone can change their nick Hostmask *!*troll@203.0.113.7 nick!user@host, with * and ? wildcards takes a new connection or address Account $a:troll anyone logged in to that services account takes registering a new account 
ops:
    - "$a:mal"
banned_users:
    - "$a:troll"
    - "*!*@203.0.113.7"

Accounts are the strongest, for bans and for ops. With nick-only ops, anyone who takes an op's nick while they're away gets op powers. With $a:mal, they'd need mal's password.

Note

Account entries need a server that supports account tags, which most modern networks do, Libera included. On a server without them, account entries never match, so use hostmasks there.

docs.title: Bans with !ban
docs.text:
!ban troll bans troll's account if they're logged in, or their username and host if not, so changing nick doesn't get around it. It can only do that if troll has spoken since the bot started. Otherwise it bans the nick and says so. Built-in commands has the details.

Host bans include the username (*!*troll@host, not *!*@host) so other people sharing a host, like everyone on a tilde server, aren't caught too. To ban a whole host, give the mask yourself: !ban *!*@203.0.113.7.

Bans made with !ban are saved to ban_file and last through restarts.

docs.title: require_account
docs.text:
With require_account on, the bot only answers people logged in to a services account. Every dodge then needs a new registered account, but guests can't use the bot.

If the server doesn't support account tags, the bot would ignore everyone. It logs an error when it connects to warn you.

docs.title: In plugins
docs.text:
Use msg.is_op to check whether the sender is an op. It understands accounts and hostmasks, where msg.nick in msg.ops only compares nicks.

@pinhook.plugin.command('!announce')
def announce(msg):
    if not msg.is_op:
        return pinhook.plugin.message('only ops can announce')
    ...

For a command that's only ever for ops, @command('!announce', ops=True) does the check for you.

docs.title: What bans don't do
docs.text: A pinhook ban only means the bot ignores someone. It doesn't kick or ban them from the channel. That's still a job for the channel's own +b bans.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
Nothing should break. Two things you might notice:

  • Plugins that use msg.bot, @register or @ops log a deprecation warning saying what to use instead (msg.bot only once per bot). They all still work. Preparing for 2.0 has the details
  • Once a plugin uses msg.store, a data/ folder appears where the bot runs, or inside bot_dir if that's set

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• pinhook.testing: a TestBot that runs your plugins without a server, so you can test them with pytest
  • msg.reply(text) and msg.send(target, text) send straight away, so a plugin can reply more than once or to several places
  • Given just the text, msg.action(text) replies where the message came from and msg.notice(text) sends the sender a notice
  • msg.account (the sender's services account) and msg.is_private
  • bot_dir keeps everything a bot uses in one folder, with plugins/, data/ and logs/ inside it. Without it, files go where they did in 1.11
  • msg.store, a dictionary each plugin can keep data in. It lasts through !reload and restarts, and is saved to data_dir automatically
  • data_dir, where plugins keep their saved data
  • plugin_config gives each plugin its own settings, as msg.config, plus a shared section every plugin can read
  • !reload also reads plugin_config from the config file again, so settings can change without a restart
  • SASL logins with sasl_password (and sasl_account if it's not the nickname). The bot is logged in before it joins channels, and gets its own nick on networks that reserve registered nicks
  • ${NAME} in a config file is filled in from the environment, so passwords don't have to be in the file
  • Docstrings for everything plugins and bot scripts use, so editors can show help, and an API reference generated from them
  • A Preparing for 2.0 guide to getting plugins ready for 2.0

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
• msg.bot, which will be read only in 2.0. Use msg.reply(), msg.send() and msg.botnick instead. It still works, and logs a warning once
  • @register and @ops now raise a DeprecationWarning too, saying what to use instead. They'll be removed in 2.0

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • The example dice plugins used an invalid escape in their regex, which newer Pythons warn about

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
• SSL now checks the server's certificate. If your bot connects to a server with a self-signed certificate, it will stop connecting until you set ssl_verify: false. The log says exactly this when it happens.
  • TwitchBot connects over SSL to irc.chat.twitch.tv on port 6697, so your oauth token isn't sent in plain text anymore.
  • Bots mark themselves as bots on servers that support it. Set bot_mode: false to turn this off.
  • !ban bans accounts and hosts, not just nicks. If the person has spoken since the bot started, !ban troll bans their account if they're logged in, or their user and host if not. Bans are now saved to <nickname>.bans.json in the bot's working directory, set ban_file: "" to keep them in memory only.
  • !banlist is ops only, since bans can now include hostmasks.
  • Log lines show which bot they came from (e.g. bot.pinbot), which adds a field to the log format. Each bot now has its own logger, log level and log file.
  • log_level: off turns logging off completely. It used to still log warnings and errors.
  • Plugins are loaded as pinhook_plugins.<filename>. This only matters if one plugin imported another by its filename.
  • If you subclass Bot: call_plugins and call_internal_commands take new arguments (botnick and op).
  • Python 3.8 or newer is required.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• ssl_verify option for servers with self-signed certificates
  • bot_mode option, sets the bot user mode the server advertises
  • ops and banned_users can use hostmasks (*!*@203.0.113.7) and services accounts ($a:troll) as well as nicks
  • ban_file option, bans made with !ban last through restarts
  • require_account option, only answers people logged in to a services account
  • msg.is_op for plugins, which understands accounts and hostmasks
  • If the bot's nick is taken when it connects, it tries nick_, nick__ and so on, instead of hanging
  • When connecting fails the log says why (bad certificate, wrong port, server name typo, connection refused) instead of retrying silently
  • Unknown options are logged with a suggestion, e.g. unknown option 'ssl_requred' ignored, did you mean 'ssl_required'?
  • TOML config files work without extra packages on Python 3.11+
  • Mistakes in a config file are listed plainly, instead of as a python traceback
  • A documentation site, at https://archangelic.github.io/pinhook/
  • Tests, and a workflow running them on Python 3.8 to 3.14 (closes #10)
  • Publishing to PyPI uses trusted publishing

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• SSL crashed on Python 3.12+
  • hide=True on commands did nothing
  • !ban didn't actually stop banned users, and bans and ops were case sensitive
  • The bot didn't ignore messages from its own nick (#75)
  • Private messages crashed the bot after its nick changed
  • A plugin returning something other than message() or action() crashed the bot
  • Newlines inside a list of output lines crashed the bot
  • A plugin named like another module (e.g. json.py) replaced that module
  • log_level crashed on capital letters or warn
  • !reload left deleted plugins behind
  • Log lines were written more than once when more than one Bot was created
  • !disable said nothing for plugins that don't exist
  • !op and !ban with no nick added an empty name
  • !quit crashed when Python's site module isn't loaded
  • The toml install hint crashed instead of showing
  • Removed the enum34 dependency, which could break Python's own enum

docs.title: Built-in commands
docs.text: Every bot has these commands. They're shown with the default ! prefix, change it with cmd_prefix.

docs.title: For everyone
docs.text: Command What it does !help Private messages the list of commands and listeners. Ops also see the op-only commands. Turn it off with disable_help

docs.title: For ops
docs.text:
Who counts as an op is set by ops.

Command What it does !join #channel [key] Join a channel, with its key if it has one !quit [message] Disconnect and stop the bot. The quit message defaults to "See y'all later!" !reload Reload every plugin from the plugin folder. Picks up new, changed and deleted plugins. Disabled plugins stay disabled, and saved plugin data is kept. If the bot was started from a config file, it also reads plugin_config from it again !enable <plugin> Turn a plugin back on !disable <plugin> Turn a plugin off without removing it !op <nick> Add a bot operator, until the bot restarts !deop <nick> Remove a bot operator, until the bot restarts !ops List bot operators !ban <nick> Make the bot ignore someone. See below !unban <nick> Remove a ban. See below !banlist List current bans

!enable and !disable take a command's name (like !roll) or a listener's name.

docs.title: !ban and !unban
docs.text:
!ban picks the hardest ban to dodge that it can:

  1. If they're logged in to a services account, it bans the account: $a:troll
  2. If not, it bans their username and host: *!*troll@203.0.113.7
  3. If they haven't spoken since the bot started, it can only ban the nick: troll

The reply says which one it used:

<mal> !ban troll
<ph-bot> mal: banned troll (account trollacct)

You can also give a hostmask or account yourself: !ban *!*@203.0.113.* or !ban $a:troll.

!unban with the nick they're using now removes whatever bans them, account and host bans included. Bans made with !ban are saved to ban_file. A ban from the config file can be lifted with !unban, but it comes back after a restart until you remove it from the config.

Bans and ops explains the kinds of entries in more detail.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
pinhook needs Python 3.8 or newer.

pip install pinhook

A bot can be started two ways: from a config file with the pinhook command, or from your own python file. Both take the same options.

docs.title: From a config file
docs.text:
Config files can be YAML, TOML or JSON.

YAMLTOMLJSON 
nickname: "ph-bot"
server: "irc.libera.chat"
port: 6697
ssl_required: true
channels:
    - "#foo"
    - "#bar"

nickname = "ph-bot"
server = "irc.libera.chat"
port = 6697
ssl_required = true
channels = ["#foo", "#bar"]

{
    "nickname": "ph-bot",
    "server": "irc.libera.chat",
    "port": 6697,
    "ssl_required": true,
    "channels": ["#foo", "#bar"]
}

nickname, server and channels are required, everything else is optional.

YAML configs need pip install pinhook[yaml]. TOML configs work out of the box on Python 3.11 and newer, older versions need pip install pinhook[toml].

Start the bot with:

pinhook config.yaml

pinhook works out the format from the file extension. If it can't, tell it with --format:

pinhook --format yaml my-bot.conf

docs.title: Passwords and other secrets
docs.text:
Keep secrets out of the config file by writing ${NAME}. pinhook fills it in from the environment variable called NAME when the bot starts:

ns_pass: "${PH_NICKSERV_PASSWORD}"

PH_NICKSERV_PASSWORD=hunter2 pinhook config.yaml

It works in any value, including inside lists and plugin settings. If the variable isn't set, the bot doesn't start, and says which one is missing. To write a literal ${ in a value, write $${. New in 1.12.

docs.title: Mistakes in the config
docs.text: If the config has a mistake pinhook stops and says which key is wrong. A key it doesn't recognise, like a typo, is logged as a warning with a suggestion instead.

docs.title: From a python file
docs.text:
from pinhook.bot import Bot

bot = Bot(
    channels=['#foo', '#bar'],
    nickname='ph-bot',
    server='irc.libera.chat',
    port=6697,
    ssl_required=True,
)
bot.start()

Bot can also be subclassed to add your own behaviour. adminbot is a good example.

docs.title: Your first plugin
docs.text:
When it starts, the bot loads every .py file in its plugin folder (plugins by default, see plugin_dir).

Save this as plugins/hello.py:

import pinhook.plugin

@pinhook.plugin.command('!hello', help_text='says hello back')
def hello(msg):
    return pinhook.plugin.message('hi {}!'.format(msg.nick))

Now !hello in a channel gets a reply, and the command shows up in !help. Change the file and an op can run !reload to pick it up without restarting the bot.

Writing plugins covers the rest: listeners, op-only commands, and everything a plugin can see about a message.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: The bot logs to the console and to <nickname>.log in the folder it runs from. See log_level and log_file to change that, and Troubleshooting for what the messages mean.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
These work the same in a config file or as keyword arguments to Bot. nickname, server and channels are required, everything here is optional.

If pinhook doesn't recognise an option it logs a warning and suggests the closest match:

unknown option 'ssl_requred' ignored, did you mean 'ssl_required'?
Option Default In short port 6667 server port ssl_required False connect over ssl ssl_verify True check the server's certificate server_pass none server password sasl_password none log in with SASL sasl_account the nickname account to log in as ns_pass none nickserv password nickserv "NickServ" nick of the nickserv service ops [] bot operators banned_users [] people the bot ignores ban_file "<nickname>.bans.json" where !ban saves bans require_account False only answer logged-in users bot_dir none one folder for everything the bot keeps plugin_dir "plugins" where plugins live plugin_config none settings for plugins data_dir "data" where plugins keep their data cmd_prefix "!" prefix for built-in commands use_prefix_for_plugins False add the prefix to plugin commands disable_help False turn off !help bot_mode True mark the bot as a bot log_level "info" how much to log log_file "<nickname>.log" where to log

docs.title: port
docs.text: The server port. Plain-text IRC is usually 6667, ssl is usually 6697.

docs.title: ssl_required
docs.text: Connect over ssl. Set port to the server's ssl port too, usually 6697.

docs.title: ssl_verify
docs.text:
Check the server's ssl certificate is valid and issued for that server name, so nobody in between can pretend to be the server. Leave this on.

Only turn it off for a server with a self-signed certificate. If the check fails, the log says why and whether turning it off would help, see Troubleshooting.

Tip

On Python 3.13 and newer you can keep checking on for a self-signed server: point the SSL_CERT_FILE environment variable at the server's certificate.

docs.title: server_pass
docs.text: Password for the server itself, if it needs one. This is not your nickserv password.

docs.title: sasl_password
docs.text:
Log in to the bot's services account with SASL, while it connects. This is the best way to log in where the server supports it, which most modern networks do, Libera included:

  • the bot is logged in before it joins any channels
  • it gets its own nick even when the network reserves registered nicks, which stops a bot that logs in later from using its nick at all
ssl_required: true
port: 6697
sasl_password: "${PH_BOT_PASSWORD}"

If the login fails, the bot logs why and connects anyway, then tries ns_pass if that's set. Use it with ssl_required, or the password is sent in plain text. The bot warns if you don't. New in 1.12.

docs.title: sasl_account
docs.text: The account to log in to with SASL, if it isn't the same as the bot's nickname. New in 1.12.

docs.title: ns_pass
docs.text: Password to identify with nickserv. The bot sends it straight after connecting. Prefer sasl_password where the server supports it. If both are set and SASL works, ns_pass isn't sent.

docs.title: nickserv
docs.text:
The nick of the nickserv service, if your network calls it something other than NickServ.

If the bot's nickname is taken when it connects, it tries nickname_, then nickname__, and so on.

docs.title: ops
docs.text:
Bot operators, who can run the op-only built-in commands and op-only plugin commands. Entries can be nicks, hostmasks or services accounts, see Bans and ops.

ops:
    - "$a:mal"

docs.title: banned_users
docs.text: People the bot ignores completely. Same kinds of entries as ops. Bans added with !ban while the bot runs are saved separately, in ban_file.

docs.title: ban_file
docs.text:
File where bans made with !ban are saved, so they last through restarts. With bot_dir set, the default is data/<nickname>.bans.json inside it. Bans from banned_users stay in the config and aren't copied into it.

Set it to "" to keep !ban bans in memory only. If the file can't be read the bot won't start, rather than quietly forgetting bans.

docs.title: require_account
docs.text: Only answer people who are logged in to a services account. This makes bans much harder to dodge, but guests can't use the bot at all. Needs a server that supports account tags, see Bans and ops.

docs.title: bot_dir
docs.text:
A folder to keep everything the bot uses in one place. With it set, the bot uses this layout:

ph-bot/                     <- bot_dir
├── plugins/                <- plugin_dir
├── data/                   <- data_dir
│   └── ph-bot.bans.json    <- ban_file
└── logs/
    └── ph-bot.log          <- log_file

Without bot_dir, files go where they always have, in the folder the bot runs from: plugins/, data/, <nickname>.log and <nickname>.bans.json.

Relative paths in plugin_dir, data_dir, log_file and ban_file are inside bot_dir when it's set, so you can still move one thing. Absolute paths stay where they point. ~ means your home folder. Folders are created when they're first needed.

Tip

Two bots can share a bot_dir. They share plugins and plugin data, but each keeps its own log and ban file, since those are named after the bot.

bot_dir is new in 1.12.

docs.title: plugin_dir
docs.text: Folder the bot loads plugins from. Every .py file in it is loaded. It's created if it doesn't exist.

docs.title: data_dir
docs.text: Folder where plugins keep their saved data, one .json file per plugin. New in 1.12.

docs.title: plugin_config
docs.text:
Settings for plugins, a section per plugin file, plus a shared section every plugin can read. See Settings.

plugin_config:
    weather:
        units: "metric"
    shared:
        modteam: ["mal", "ana"]

A section for a plugin that isn't loaded logs a warning, with a suggestion if it looks like a typo. New in 1.12.

docs.title: cmd_prefix
docs.text: Prefix for the built-in commands, so "?" makes it ?help, ?reload and so on.

docs.title: use_prefix_for_plugins
docs.text: Add cmd_prefix to plugin commands too. With it on, @command('roll') answers to !roll. With it off, plugins choose their own command word, prefix and all.

docs.title: disable_help
docs.text: Turn off the built-in !help command, for example when a plugin provides its own.

docs.title: bot_mode
docs.text: Mark the bot as a bot on servers that support it, so /whois shows it as one. pinhook sets whichever user mode the server advertises for this (IRCv3 bot mode), and does nothing on servers that don't.

docs.title: log_level
docs.text: One of "debug", "info", "warning", "error" or "critical", in any case. "off" turns logging off completely.

docs.title: log_file
docs.text:
File to write logs to. With bot_dir set, the default is logs/<nickname>.log inside it. Each bot has its own log file and log level, even several bots in one python process. Log lines name the bot they came from:

2026-10-27 22:33:18,491 - INFO - bot.ph-bot - bot - setting bot mode +B

docs.title: Writing plugins
docs.text:
A plugin is a .py file in the bot's plugin folder with one or more decorated functions in it. There are two kinds:

  • Commands run when a message starts with their command word, like !roll 2d6
  • Listeners see every message that isn't a command, and decide for themselves what to do

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
import random

import pinhook.plugin

@pinhook.plugin.command('!roll', help_text='roll a die, or !roll 20 for a d20')
def roll(msg):
    sides = int(msg.arg) if msg.arg.isdigit() else 6
    return pinhook.plugin.message('{} rolled a {}'.format(msg.nick, random.randint(1, sides)))

The function gets one argument, the message. msg.arg holds everything after the command word.

@command takes:

Argument Default What it does help_text 'N/A' shown next to the command in !help ops False only ops can run it ops_msg '' what anyone else gets told when they try. Empty means no reply hide False leave it out of !help 
@pinhook.plugin.command('!shutdown-games', ops=True, ops_msg='only ops can do that')
def shutdown_games(msg):
    return pinhook.plugin.message('games are closed for tonight')

@pinhook.plugin.command('!secret', hide=True)
def secret(msg):
    return pinhook.plugin.message('you found it!')

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
A listener is given a name instead of a command word. It's called for every message that isn't a command, including /me actions, and returns nothing when it has nothing to say.

import pinhook.plugin

@pinhook.plugin.listener('hello')
def say_hi(msg):
    if 'hello' in msg.text.lower():
        return pinhook.plugin.message('hi {}!'.format(msg.nick))

docs.title: Replying
docs.text:
There are two ways to reply: return what to say, or say it straight away.

Return one of these to reply where the message came from, the channel or the private message:

  • pinhook.plugin.message(text): a normal message
  • pinhook.plugin.action(text): a /me action

Both take a string or a list of strings. Each line is sent as its own message, with a short pause between lines so the bot doesn't flood the channel.

return pinhook.plugin.message(['line one', 'line two'])

Returning anything else, like a plain string, is logged as an error and nothing is sent.

Or use the message's methods, which send straight away, so a plugin can reply more than once or send to several places:

Method Sends msg.reply(text) a message where this one came from msg.action(text) a /me action where this one came from msg.notice(text) a notice to the sender only msg.send(target, text) a message to another channel or nick msg.action(target, text) a /me action to another channel or nick msg.notice(target, text) a notice to another channel or nick 
@pinhook.plugin.command('!countdown')
def countdown(msg):
    msg.reply('3... 2... 1...')
    msg.send('#announcements', 'liftoff in {}'.format(msg.channel))
    msg.notice('thanks for launching!')

They get the same line splitting and flood protection as returned replies. msg.reply, msg.send and the one-argument forms are new in 1.12. msg.privmsg(target, text) still works too.

docs.title: The message
docs.text:
Attribute What it is nick who sent it user the username part of their hostmask (nick!user@host) account the services account they're logged in to, or None. Needs a server with account tags, see Bans and ops channel where it was sent. For a private message, the sender's nick is_private True if it was a private message to the bot cmd (commands) the command word that triggered it arg (commands) everything after the command word text (listeners) the whole message msg_type "message", or "action" for a /me nick_list nicks in the channel. Just the sender for private messages is_op True if the sender is a bot operator. Understands accounts and hostmasks, so use it rather than nick in msg.ops ops the list of bot operators, as written in the config botnick the bot's current nick store the plugin's saved data, see Saving data config the plugin's settings, see Settings logger the bot's logger, see Logging datetime when the message arrived, a timezone-aware datetime timestamp the same as a unix timestamp bot the bot itself. Deprecated, see Preparing for 2.0

account, is_private, store and config are new in 1.12.

docs.title: Saving data
docs.text:
msg.store is a dictionary the plugin can keep things in. It's still there in the next message, after !reload and after the bot restarts:

@pinhook.plugin.command('!karma')
def karma(msg):
    scores = msg.store.setdefault('scores', {})
    scores[msg.arg] = scores.get(msg.arg, 0) + 1
    return pinhook.plugin.message('{} has {} karma'.format(msg.arg, scores[msg.arg]))
  • Each plugin file has its own store, named after the file. Commands and listeners in the same file share it
  • The bot saves it after each plugin call if anything changed, including changes inside nested lists and dicts. There's nothing to call
  • It's saved as <plugin file name>.json in data_dir, so karma.py keeps its data in data/karma.json
  • Values have to be things JSON can hold: strings, numbers, lists, dicts, True, False and None. Keys are saved as strings. Store a datetime as a string or a timestamp

Stores are meant for small things: scores, quotes, last-seen times, settings changed by a command. For lots of data or lots of writes, use a proper database like sqlite3.

To clear a plugin's data, stop the bot and delete its file.

msg.store is new in 1.12.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
msg.config holds the plugin's settings, from plugin_config in the bot's config. Owners can change them without editing the plugin:

plugin_config:
    weather:
        api_key: "${WEATHER_API_KEY}"
        units: "metric"
    shared:
        modteam: ["mal", "ana"]

@pinhook.plugin.command('!weather')
def weather(msg):
    key = msg.config['api_key']
    units = msg.config.get('units', 'metric')
    ...
  • Each plugin reads the section named after its file, so weather.py reads weather
  • msg.config.shared is the shared section, which every plugin can read. Use it for settings several plugins need
  • Settings are read only. For things the plugin changes itself, use msg.store
  • After changing settings in the config file, an op can run !reload to use them without restarting. If the file has a mistake, the bot keeps the old settings and says so. Other options, like server, still need a restart
  • A missing setting fails with a message naming it: plugin_config has no 'api_key' setting for the weather plugin. Use msg.config.get('name', default) for optional ones

msg.config is new in 1.12.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Use msg.logger so a plugin's logs go to its bot's log file at its bot's log level:

msg.logger.info('rolled {} for {}'.format(result, msg.nick))

If a plugin raises an exception, the bot logs it with the traceback and carries on.

docs.title: Loading and reloading
docs.text:
Every .py file in the plugin folder is loaded when the bot starts. An op can run !reload to pick up new, changed and deleted plugins without restarting, and !disable or !enable to switch one off and on.

Plugin files are loaded as pinhook_plugins.<filename>, so a plugin named after another module, like json.py, is fine.

docs.title: Testing plugins
docs.text: pinhook.testing runs your plugins in a bot that never connects, so you can check what they reply with pytest. See Testing plugins.

docs.title: Preparing for 2.0
docs.text:
pinhook 2.0 will change how plugins talk to the bot. 1.12 adds the new ways alongside the old ones, so you can update your plugins now, one at a time, and they'll keep working in both.

Nothing here is urgent. Plugins written for 1.11 work in 1.12 unchanged, and the old ways log a warning saying what to use instead.

docs.title: What to change
Finding what needs changing
docs.text:
Run your plugin tests with deprecation warnings turned into errors. Each warning points at the line in your plugin that needs changing:

pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning

No tests yet? Testing plugins shows how to write them with TestBot.

On a running bot, each deprecation is logged once, as a warning:

WARNING - bot.ph-bot - bot - msg.bot is deprecated and will be read only in 2.0, use msg.reply(), msg.send() and msg.botnick instead

docs.title: What's planned for 2.0
docs.text:
These are plans, not promises yet. They might change before 2.0 is released.

  • msg.bot becomes read only: plugins can look at the bot's nick and channels, but not reach into it
  • @register and @ops are removed
  • replies don't block: the bot can answer other people while a plugin sends a long reply
  • commands are written without their prefix, and the bot's config chooses the prefix
  • 1.x plugins still run in 2.0 through a compatibility layer, with warnings

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Everything a plugin or bot script uses, generated from pinhook's own code. For how to use it, with examples, see Writing plugins, Testing plugins and Options.

docs.title: Message
docs.text:
A message sent to the bot, as a plugin gets it.

Attributes:

Name Type Description nick

who sent it.

user

the username part of their hostmask (nick!user@host).

account

the services account they're logged in to, or None.

channel

where it was sent. For a private message, the sender's nick.

is_private

True if it was a private message to the bot.

cmd

(commands) the command word that triggered it.

arg

(commands) everything after the command word.

text

(listeners) the whole message.

msg_type

'message', or 'action' for a /me.

nick_list

nicks in the channel. Just the sender for private messages.

is_op

True if the sender is a bot operator.

ops

the list of bot operators, as written in the config.

botnick

the bot's current nick.

store

the plugin's saved data, a dict kept between restarts.

config

the plugin's settings from plugin_config, read only.

logger

the bot's logger.

datetime

when the message arrived, a timezone-aware datetime.

timestamp

the same as a unix timestamp.

docs.title: Store
docs.text:
Bases: dict

A plugin's saved data: a dict that's kept between messages, reloads and restarts.

Plugins get theirs as msg.store. The bot saves it after each plugin call if anything in it changed, nested changes included.

Values have to be things JSON can hold: strings, numbers, lists, dicts, True, False and None. Keys are saved as strings.

docs.title: save_if_changed
docs.text:
save_if_changed()

Save the store if anything in it changed since it was last saved.

docs.title: PluginConfig
docs.text:
Bases: Mapping

A plugin's settings from plugin_config in the bot's config. Read only.

Plugins get theirs as msg.config: their own section, keyed by plugin file name, and msg.config.shared for the section every plugin can read.

docs.title: TestBot
docs.text:
Bases: Bot

A Bot that never connects, for testing plugins.

Plugins, ops, bans and the built-in commands all work as they do on a real server. What the bot sends is recorded in sent instead, and a plugin that raises an exception fails the test with a PluginError.

docs.title: Testing plugins
docs.text:
pinhook.testing runs your plugins in a bot that never connects to a server, so you can test them with pytest or any other test runner.

from pinhook.testing import TestBot

def test_roll():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_dir='plugins')
    assert bot.say('!roll 1d1') == ['1']

TestBot is a real Bot. Plugins, ops, bans and the built-in commands all work the way they do on a server. The difference is that what the bot sends is recorded for you to check, flood protection pauses are skipped, and no log or ban files are written.

Note

TestBot is new in 1.12.

docs.title: Talking to the bot
docs.text:
Three methods send the bot a message and return its replies, as a list of strings:

Method Sends Returns the replies sent to bot.say(text) a message in a channel that channel bot.action(text) a /me action in a channel that channel bot.private(text) a private message to the bot the sender

Replies include both messages and actions. Each takes the same optional arguments:

  • nick: who's talking (default: 'tester')
  • channel: which channel, for say and action (default: the bot's first channel, '#test')
  • user and host: the rest of their hostmask (default: the nick, and 'example.com')
  • account: the services account they're logged in to (default: none)
def test_greeting():
    bot = TestBot()
    assert bot.say('hello everyone', nick='mal') == ['hi mal!']
    assert bot.say('hello', channel='#other') == ['hi tester!']

docs.title: Checking everything that was sent
docs.text:
bot.sent is everything the bot has sent, as Sent(kind, target, text) entries, where kind is 'message', 'action' or 'notice'. Use it to check notices, or messages a plugin sent somewhere else:

from pinhook.testing import Sent, TestBot

def test_whisper():
    bot = TestBot()
    bot.say('!whisper', nick='mal')
    assert Sent('notice', 'mal', 'psst') in bot.sent

bot.sent_to(target) returns the text of every message and action sent to one place. !help, for example, replies privately, so check it like this:

def test_help_lists_roll():
    bot = TestBot()
    bot.say('!help', nick='mal')
    assert '!roll -- roll some dice' in bot.sent_to('mal')

docs.title: Saved data
docs.text:
A TestBot keeps plugin stores in memory, so nothing is written to disk. Look at one with bot.store(name), where name is the plugin's file name:

def test_karma_is_counted():
    bot = TestBot()
    bot.say('!karma pinhook')
    bot.say('!karma pinhook')
    assert bot.store('karma') == {'scores': {'pinhook': 2}}

Saving something JSON can't hold, like a datetime, fails the test with a PluginError.

docs.title: Options, ops and bans
docs.text:
TestBot takes any of the bot's options, so you can test ops and bans the same way they're set up for real:

def test_only_ops_can_announce():
    bot = TestBot(ops=['$a:mal'])
    assert bot.say('!announce hi', nick='mal', account='mal') == ['announced']
    assert bot.say('!announce hi', nick='mal') == ['only ops can announce']

Plugin settings work the same way:

def test_weather_uses_the_api_key():
    bot = TestBot(plugin_config={'weather': {'api_key': 'test-key'}})
    ...

It also takes nickname (default: 'testbot') and channels (default: ['#test']).

docs.title: When a plugin breaks
docs.text:
On a real server, a plugin that raises an exception is logged and the bot carries on. In a TestBot it fails the test instead: you get a PluginError with the original exception and its traceback attached. The same happens when a plugin returns something other than message() or action(), or when a plugin file can't be loaded at all. That one fails as soon as you create the TestBot.

import pytest
from pinhook.testing import PluginError, TestBot

def test_zero_sided_dice_crash():
    bot = TestBot()
    with pytest.raises(PluginError):
        bot.say('!roll 1d0')

Turning logging off with log_level='off' turns this off too, because the errors are caught from the bot's log.

docs.title: Other things to know
docs.text:
• bot.pauses lists the flood protection pauses the bot would have taken, in seconds
  • !quit raises SystemExit, so wrap it in pytest.raises(SystemExit). bot.quit_message holds the message it quit with
  • !join adds the channel to bot.channels
  • plugins are shared by every bot in the same python process, so make one TestBot at a time

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Most problems show up in the bot's log, on the console and in log_file. Set log_level to "debug" to see every message the bot receives and what it does with it.

docs.title: Starting up
docs.text: Message What to do config.yaml has problems: followed by a list Fix each key it lists. It names the key and what's wrong with its value unknown option 'x' ignored, did you mean 'y'? A typo, or an option that doesn't exist. The bot still starts, without it log_level must be one of: ... Use one of the listed levels couldn't read ban file ... The ban file isn't valid JSON. Fix or remove it. The bot won't start rather than lose the bans in it ban file ... should be a list of ban entries The ban file should look like ["troll", "$a:troll"] could not load plugin That plugin has an error. The traceback under it says where. The other plugins still load

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
pinhook keeps retrying every 1 to 5 minutes when it can't connect, and logs why each time:

Message says What to do the server's ssl certificate failed verification (...). If this server uses a self-signed certificate, set ssl_verify to false The certificate isn't signed by anyone your system trusts. If it's self-signed on purpose, set ssl_verify to false ... Set server to the name the certificate was issued for, not an IP address or alias The certificate is fine, but for a different name. Use the server's real name in server ... This needs fixing on the server The server's certificate has expired. Tell its admins ssl handshake failed (...). Check 6667 is the server's ssl port, usually 6697 ssl_required is on but port is the plain-text port server name not found, check the server setting A typo in server, or no network connection refused, check the server and port settings Nothing is listening on that port

Once connected:

Message What it means nickname x in use, trying x_ Someone else has the nick, so the bot picked a new one. If the nick is the bot's own registered one, the network is probably keeping it for whoever logs in to that account: use sasl_password so the bot logs in while it connects logged in as x with SASL All good: the bot is logged in to its account SASL login as x failed (...), check sasl_account and sasl_password The server turned the login down, and its reason is in brackets. The bot connects anyway, without its account sasl_password is set, but this server doesn't offer SASL PLAIN logins Use ns_pass on this server instead sasl_password will be sent without ssl Turn on ssl_required, and set port to the ssl port require_account is on but this server doesn't tell the bot who is logged in (account-tag), so the bot will ignore everyone Turn off require_account on this server

docs.title: The bot doesn't answer
docs.text:
Work through these in order:

  1. Is it a command? Commands only run when the message starts with the command word exactly. Check !help
  2. Is the plugin loaded and enabled? !help lists commands and listeners. An op can !enable a disabled one
  3. Are you banned? An op can check !banlist. Bans can match accounts and hostmasks, not just nicks
  4. Is require_account on? Then you need to be logged in to a services account
  5. Did the plugin fail? Look for issue with command !x or issue with listener x in the log, with a traceback under it

docs.title: Plugin messages
docs.text: Message What it means issue with command !x / issue with listener x The plugin raised an exception. The traceback under it says where plugins must return message() or action(), got str The plugin returned a plain string. Wrap it: return pinhook.plugin.message(text) output message too long: ... One line was over IRC's 512-byte limit, so it and the lines after it weren't sent. Split long output into a list of lines @register is deprecated and will be removed in 2.0 ... Swap @register('!x') for @command('!x') @ops is deprecated and will be removed in 2.0 ... Swap @ops('!x', 'msg') for @command('!x', ops=True, ops_msg='msg') msg.bot is deprecated and will be read only in 2.0 ... See Preparing for 2.0 for what to use instead

docs.title: Twitch bots
docs.text:
pinhook has a bot class made for Twitch chat:

from pinhook.bot import TwitchBot

bot = TwitchBot(
    nickname='ph-bot',
    channel='#channel',
    token='super-secret-oauth-token'
)
bot.start()

token is the bot account's oauth token, without the oauth: part. TwitchBot always connects to irc.chat.twitch.tv over ssl, so the token isn't sent in plain text.

Plugins work exactly the same as on IRC.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
TwitchBot takes fewer options, since Twitch handles the server and ssl:

  • port (default: 6697)
  • ops
  • banned_users
  • ban_file
  • plugin_dir
  • cmd_prefix
  • use_prefix_for_plugins
  • disable_help
  • bot_mode
  • log_level
  • log_file

Twitch doesn't have services accounts, so use nicks in ops and banned_users. Twitch usernames can't be changed freely like IRC nicks can.

docs.title: Upgrading to 1.11
docs.text: Most bots upgrade with no changes. Check this list for the ones that might affect yours. The changelog has everything that changed.

docs.title: Might need a change
docs.text:
Your server uses a self-signed ssl certificate. pinhook now checks certificates, so the bot stops connecting until you set ssl_verify to false. The log says exactly this when it happens.

You're on Python 3.7 or older. pinhook now needs 3.8 or newer.

A plugin imports another plugin by its filename. Plugins are now loaded as pinhook_plugins.<filename>, so import dice from another plugin no longer works.

Your Bot subclass overrides call_plugins or call_internal_commands. Both take new arguments: botnick and op.

Something parses the bot's log lines. Lines now include the bot's logger name, like bot.ph-bot, before the module name.

docs.title: Works differently, nothing to change
docs.text:
• TwitchBot connects over ssl to irc.chat.twitch.tv on port 6697.
  • Bots mark themselves as bots on servers that support it. Set bot_mode to false to stop that.
  • !ban bans accounts and hosts, not just nicks, and saves bans to <nickname>.bans.json in the folder the bot runs from. See Bans and ops.
  • !banlist is ops only, since bans can now include hostmasks.
  • log_level: off turns logging off completely. It used to still log warnings and errors.
  • Each bot has its own logger, log level and log file, so several bots in one process no longer share them.

docs.title: Worth doing
docs.text:
• Use accounts for ops: $a:yourname instead of a nick, so nobody can borrow an op's nick. See Bans and ops.
  • Use msg.is_op in plugins instead of msg.nick in msg.ops.
  • Swap @register and @ops for @command. They'll be removed in 2.0. Preparing for 2.0 lists everything worth changing.
